title: One spritesheet vs 16 separate image files, on tiles rebuilt every frame
variable: single atlas texture vs one texture per sprite, tiles destroyed and recreated
claim: The companion to many-images-vs-spritesheet, which asked the same question of a settled scene and found no reliable difference at 30 or 100 tiles and Paint 1.69x at 300. Its own result names the gap this case fills: 'this measures steady-state drawing only... not load time or memory'. png-vs-svg-churn-complex then showed that for an image asset the cost overwhelmingly lands at ELEMENT CREATION rather than in steady-state frames - 462x on Styles under churn against 2.81x on Paint standing still. That makes creation the axis on which atlasing is most likely to earn its keep, and the one nobody has measured. If binding 16 textures instead of 1 costs anything when the referencing elements are built, this is where it shows. Read with many-images-vs-spritesheet: a null in both says atlasing buys nothing at runtime below 300 tiles and the case for it rests entirely on texture memory and Instaload entries, neither of which this lab can see.
result: NOT CONFIRMED on the hypothesized axis, and that is the finding. Styles - where png-vs-svg-churn-complex found 462x for a vector asset - is FLAT at every count here: 1.11x at 30, 0.86x at 100, 1.02x at 300. Delivering the same artwork as 16 textures instead of 1 costs nothing when the referencing elements are created. The only thing that moves is Paint, 2.04x / 3.17x / 2.14x, and in absolute terms that is 0.25-0.39ms rising to 0.54-0.80ms - sub-millisecond at every count, on pages holding a steady 161 frames per trace in both variants. READ THE RATIOS, NOT THE VERDICT on the 300 row: the headline says 'B costs less (Script-bound)' because Script fell 5.57ms to 4.83ms, a larger per-frame move than Paint's +0.29ms, and the verdict names whichever phase moved furthest. Paint is consistently 2-3x worse for loose files at every count; the Script dip is not a reason to ship them. COLD LOAD, measured separately with cold-load-probe.mjs and NOT a row here: 16 texture uploads against 1 cost a peak frame of 4.24-4.45ms Paint against 1.28-3.58ms, with both variants holding 194 frames and neither hitching. That is a difference of one to three milliseconds, paid once. For scale, the same probe on the same 300 tiles measured a 977ms frozen frame for a complex SVG. TAKEN WITH many-images-vs-spritesheet, which found nothing at 30 or 100 and Paint 1.69x at 300 on a settled scene, the picture is consistent: atlasing is a small drawing-side win and nothing else. It is not a creation-time win and not a load-time win. THE CASE FOR ATLASING THEREFORE RESTS ON WHAT THIS LAB CANNOT MEASURE - texture memory and Instaload entry count, which RAG 15-tooling.md names as the real risk. A null here is not a licence to ship loose sprites; it means the runtime argument for atlasing is weak and the memory argument is the one to make.
notes: Applicability gate: ADAPTED - see the adaptation below. url(), background-position, createElement/removeChild/appendChild are all supported and were already verified against the Player by many-images-vs-spritesheet and pool-vs-create. THE ADAPTATION, and why: the lab reports steady-state MEDIANS over a 5s window, so a rebuild at a realistic rate would fall outside the median and both variants would report their idle frames - a confident, false NO RELIABLE DIFFERENCE (AUTHORING.md rule 6, the duty-cycle trap). The rebuild therefore runs every frame in both variants. Read the ratio as the cost per rebuild, NOT as the cost of any real UI. Rule 1: one variable, how many textures the same artwork is delivered in - identical to many-images-vs-spritesheet, so the two cases are directly comparable and differ only in what drives the damage. The churn is the driver here, not the variable: it is byte-identical in A and B. Rule 2: identical DOM at the end of every frame - same node count, same classes, same positions, and PIXEL-IDENTICAL output, since the atlas and the 16 loose files are emitted by tools/make-baked-images.js from the same spriteAt() function. Rule 3: identical JS apart from the single USE_SHEET constant; both pages define both paths and both set backgroundImage inline, so the inline-style machinery is exercised equally. Rule 4 EXCEPTION: the two variants load different assets - that IS the variable. The 16 sprites are deliberately distinct from one another so the engine cannot dedupe them into a single texture and quietly erase the difference being measured. Rule 5: 300 tiles occupy 1852x1032 inside 1920x1080. Rule 6: the churn replaces the root-nudge driver and starts at load with no idle window. Rule 7: sprite choice derives from the loop index; no randomness. Rule 8: counts 30/100/300 tiles drawn, against a fixed 16 distinct sprites. Rule 9: plain HTML/CSS/JS. Rule 10: expected axis is Styles, following pool-vs-create and png-vs-svg-churn-complex - what a recreated node costs in cohtml is resolving its style from scratch, and a background-image is resolved there. Paint is the plausible alternative, since that is where many-images-vs-spritesheet found its only effect. LIMIT: this measures per-rebuild cost. Texture memory and Instaload entry count are what atlasing is really sold on, and no row in this lab can see either.
